source.title: Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models
source.authors: Bryan Kelly; S. Malamud; Johannes Schwab; T. Xu

record.tranche_reason: The paper does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws. It does compare downstream benchmark and economic outcomes across model scales, which bears conceptually on V6.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work as motivation and reports downstream outcomes for scaled point-in-time models. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, predictions from smaller runs, or a compute-optimal allocation. The benchmark table has no PIT-4B values for BoolQ, WinoGrande, or OpenBookQA.
record.test_reason: This is a model-release and application paper. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann to frame the point-in-time (PIT) performance gap as a scale deficit, then reports how its own PIT models perform. It fits no scaling law and reports no held-out loss. It does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. The only within-family size comparison is two models (PIT-1.5B on 170B tokens with 52 layers and width 1536; PIT-4B on 1T tokens with 20 layers and width 4096), so parameters, data and architecture all change at once. The Sharpe comparisons are against ChronoGPT, a different model family and training pipeline. Neither supports a claim of predictable scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that much of the cost of point-in-time training reflects a scale deficit. Their 4B model trained on 1T tokens approaches Gemma-3-4B and LLaMA-7B on benchmarks, though a gap remains on reasoning-heavy tasks. PIT embeddings give positive out-of-sample Sharpe ratios, stronger for larger models than ChronoGPT. The PIT models also give results close to temporally invalid full-sample models, and in the fine-tuned pair (PIT-4B-FT 1.18 vs FT-full 0.82) higher. They do not test scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper scales point-in-time models and reports benchmark and economic outcomes; it does not use the original sources' held-out-loss fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: PIT-4B (4.2B parameters, 1T tokens) beats PIT-1.5B (170B tokens) on all seven zero-shot benchmarks (average 58.1 vs 53.8). PIT-4B embeddings also give higher Sharpe ratios (1.02 to 1.18) than ChronoGPT (0.27 to 0.67).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger, longer-trained models from the same pipeline score higher on downstream benchmarks. This is a two-point comparison with parameters, data and architecture confounded, and is not evidence of predictability.

record.code_released: Public GitHub release stated, but URL not stated
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: Only two PIT model sizes are evaluated; no loss scaling fit, held-out loss results, compute sweep, or prediction from smaller runs is reported. Language benchmark evaluations are deterministic and reported without error bars. The economic evaluation uses a single dataset and portfolio framework, as the authors note.
record.rows_left_out: Left out individual benchmark results for DatedGPT, ChronoGPT, Gemma, and LLaMA, plus PIT-4B IFEval results: these do not provide the PIT model-size comparison used for the V6 rows. Table 2 and Figure 2.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
Shape changes between the two models but parameter count is not held fixed.
No power-law fits in other regimes or modalities.
No fitted or predictive relation between downstream performance and scale or loss. Only a confounded two-model comparison and cross-family Sharpe comparisons.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 is column-flattened in the text. Reconstructing the averages (PIT-4B: 406.8/7 = 58.1; PIT-1.5B: 376.4/7 = 53.8; DatedGPT four-benchmark average 52.6) shows that DatedGPT, not PIT-4B, lacks BoolQ, WinoGrande and OBQA. Rows r1, r4 and r7 carry PIT-4B's values. The correct PIT-1.5B values are 61.9, 59.4 and 34.8, and PIT-4B rows for 63.0, 64.2 and 39.0 are missing. The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped: two confounded points and cross-family Sharpe comparisons do not test predictable downstream scaling.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
Architecture details differ between models, but the paper does not hold parameter count fixed to test the effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices.
The study uses point-in-time text pretraining and instruction fine-tuning, but does not test whether power-law scaling holds in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports selected downstream comparisons, not a fitted predictive relationship with scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or scaling-law exponents, and no test of curves bending away from a power law.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: PIT model-size comparison on the reported zero-shot benchmark results and PIT economic evaluation versus ChronoGPT
reader_labels.reason: The PIT-4B average benchmark score exceeds PIT-1.5B, the reported individual benchmark scores are higher where both are shown, and PIT-4B Sharpe ratios exceed the ChronoGPT values; see r2–r13 and r14–r17.
